title: Biodiversity offsetting

definition.text: A system, used mainly by planning authorities and developers, for fully compensating the harm a development does to biodiversity.

facts.text: Offsets are measurable conservation gains designed to make up for significant harm left over after prevention and mitigation; the aim is no net loss of biodiversity, ideally a net gain.
Offsetting is the last step of the mitigation hierarchy: harm must first be avoided, minimised and reversed before what remains is offset.
Practitioners measure the amount, type and quality of habitat a project will damage, then find receptor sites where the same can be re-created.
Offsets must show additionality: a gain in biodiversity that would not have happened anyway.
As of 2019, over 100 countries had or were developing offset policies and more than 37 required offsets by law.
England's Biodiversity Net Gain rule, in force from February 2024, requires developers to show a 10% net gain in biodiversity to get planning permission.
Evidence is mixed: offsets work better in simpler, fast-recovering habitats such as wetlands, and a review found about one-third of policies and offsets reported achieving no net loss.
Critics call offsetting a "licence to trash" that legitimises habitat destruction, and question whether biodiversity in one place can be swapped for biodiversity elsewhere.

contested_note: Supporters and opponents disagree on whether offsets are feasible or ethical, given the difficulty of measuring biodiversity and swapping it between places.

title: Biodiversity banking

definition.text: A market-based form of biodiversity offsetting in which conservation gains are turned into credits that developers can buy to offset their damage.

facts.text: It is also called habitat banking, conservation banking, mitigation banking or biodiversity trading, depending on what is being conserved and where.
At a bank site, work such as reintroducing native plants, removing invasive species or filling ditches to restore a swamp generates credits for gains that would not otherwise happen.
It turns offsets into tradeable assets by creating credits in advance of a development and away from its site.
It grew out of US wetland mitigation banking in the 1980s, which arose from the no net loss policies of the 1970s Clean Water Act.
A bank's land is usually locked in by a conservation easement or covenant that binds future owners, often with a trust fund for long-term management.
More than 100 countries require biodiversity offsetting, but banking frameworks are less widespread.
A 2006 analysis of Canadian habitat banking found 25% of projects achieved no net loss of habitat productivity and 12% a net gain.

notes: Challenges section: deep uncertainties in measurement and credit issuance and risks of commodifying nature (c943d1614287).

definition.text: A biodiversity offset that prevents ecological damage that would almost certainly have happened, rather than restoring or creating habitat.

facts.text: Examples include creating protected areas, removing invasive species, or offering alternative livelihoods to stop deforestation.
Activities without a measurable gain for biodiversity, such as funding general research, do not count as offsets.
Poorly designed offset policies can create perverse incentives that encourage further biodiversity decline.

definition.text: Land offered by a company or individual for payment in return for creating or restoring wildlife habitat to offset damage elsewhere.

facts.text: The habitat work is paid for by developers seeking to offset their impact.
The biodiversity gained at the receptor site should equal or exceed the loss at the original impact site.

definition.text: A unit representing the cost of re-creating a piece of damaged habitat, which developers can buy to offset their impact on biodiversity.

facts.text: Receptor-site land is also valued in credits, covering both the cost of restoring habitat and its long-term management.
This lets developers buy and landowners sell credits, creating a market for keeping and restoring habitat.

definition.text: A market-based system of debits and credits, used mainly in the United States, in which wetlands are restored, created or enhanced to make up for unavoidable damage to wetlands elsewhere.

facts.text: Mitigation banks are sites where wetland projects are carried out before the damage they compensate for; their results become credits that developers can buy.
It grew from compensatory mitigation under section 404 of the US Clean Water Act, aiming at "no net loss of wetlands".
The first wetland mitigation banks were set up in the early 1980s following 1983 guidance from the US Fish and Wildlife Service.
Regulators often require more habitat than is damaged, a mitigation ratio, which serves the public interest.
Credits are released in stages as a bank meets performance milestones over an establishment period of about 10 to 12 years.
By 2024 more than 1200 mitigation banks were operating in the US, with 750,000 credits approved.
Studies suggest a significant share of compensation sites fail to meet administrative and ecological performance standards.

definition.text: Measures that restore, create, enhance or preserve wetlands to make up for damage that cannot be avoided; the US term for biodiversity offsetting.

facts.text: It applies only after the mitigation sequence of avoid, minimise, then compensate has been followed.
It can be on-site, on or next to the damaged area, or off-site.
Besides banks, it can be done through in-lieu fee programmes, where permittees pay into an approved fund, or permittee-responsible projects, where they do and answer for the work themselves.
Revised US rules in 2008 made mitigation banks the preferred method of compensatory mitigation.

title: Conservation easement

definition.text: A voluntary legal agreement between a landowner and a government agency or conservation group that restricts future development on a site, setting it aside permanently for conservation.

facts.text: In the US, land used for mitigation banking must be protected by a conservation easement.
The commitment binds future owners of the land, and a trust fund may pay for long-term management.
Landowners may see the permanent restriction as a drawback because it limits future uses and can lower land value.
It 'runs with the land', binding present and future owners, and is usually permanent.

contested_note: Critics say easement tax deductions are abused as a tax avoidance scheme, and US courts have penalised overstated easement values.

title: Conservation banking

definition.text: A market-based method of offsetting harm to threatened or endangered species protected under the US Endangered Species Act by creating conservation banks.

facts.text: Conservation banks are permanently protected parcels of land managed to keep endangered species and their habitat alive.
Developers who must harm protected species can buy credits from a bank instead of protecting small patches themselves.
Pooling mitigation into larger reserves gives better habitat and connectivity than small isolated patches, and is cheaper to maintain.
California created the first conservation bank in 1995 and leads with over 30; the nation's 130 banks protect over 160,000 acres.
Credit prices are set largely by supply and demand and range from $1500 for a Gopher Tortoise to $325,000 for vernal pool preservation.
Unlike wetland mitigation banking, conservation banking does not require no net loss.

notes: Conservation banking lead says its intention is no net loss (b464313919bb), while Biodiversity banking says it does not require no net loss (8b3b265c21cf); verification pass may want to look. Also: origin given as 'wetland mitigation banks created in the early 1990s' (dfd9181798ea) vs 1980s on Mitigation banking page.

title: Biodiversity Impact Credit

definition.text: A transferable biodiversity credit designed to reduce the global risk of species extinction.

facts.text: Its metric, developed by academics at Queen Mary University of London and Bar-Ilan University, measures how interventions change the average long-term survival chances of species.
For each species it adds up the change in global population divided by the current population, so restoring one threatened species from near zero gives about one credit.
It targets Target 4 of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework on cutting extinction risk, and the TNFD recommends its use.
Critics of biodiversity credits say monetising nature oversimplifies it and that credits can be used for greenwashing or merely to offset damage.

contested_note: Critics say pricing nature through credits oversimplifies it and invites greenwashing, while proponents point to growing private investment.

title: Environmental mitigation

definition.text: The process of applying measures to avoid, minimise or compensate for harm to the environment.

facts.text: In planning such as Environmental Impact Assessments it is usually guided by the mitigation hierarchy: avoid, reduce, restore, and offset.
In practice it means creating new habitat, restoring degraded habitat, or protecting existing habitat to offset harm that cannot be avoided or reduced.
It is broader than climate change mitigation, which focuses only on cutting net greenhouse gas emissions.
191 UN member states have Environmental Impact Assessment laws and more than 108 countries have biodiversity offsetting policies.
In the US, the Fish and Wildlife Coordination Act of 1934 first expressed a legal duty to minimise and compensate for environmental harm.
Its usual goals are no net loss or a net positive impact on biodiversity.

contested_note: Whether aims like no net loss and tools like offsetting advance or undermine conservation goals is disputed.

title: Mitigation hierarchy

definition.text: A sequence of steps (avoid, minimise, restore, then offset) applied in order to reduce a project's harm to the environment until none remains.

facts.text: Avoiding harm is the first step and widely seen as the most important.
Minimising reduces harm that cannot be avoided; restoring helps damaged ecosystems recover; offsetting compensates for whatever harm remains.
Offsetting is the "final resort" in the hierarchy.
It is commonly built into Environmental Impact Assessment and licensing rules, and some jurisdictions require it by law.
France writes it into law as the ERC sequence: avoid, reduce, compensate.
Versions have been proposed for waste, food waste, energy and carbon, and extensions such as the Mitigation and Conservation Hierarchy.

notes: Also drafted from the phrase dossier phrase-offsets-and-banking (Mitigation hierarchy); not repeated in part90.

title: Environmental crediting system

definition.text: A system set up by a governing body that allocates debits for planned environmental damage and credits for conservation gains, so damage can be offset by buying credits.

facts.text: Credits come from banks where a resource has been improved; debits arise where significant harm is planned at a permitted site.
Biodiversity banking and its forms, such as mitigation, habitat, species and conservation banking, are examples.
Key difficulties are choosing the unit of exchange, making debits and credits ecologically equivalent, and proving additionality.

contested_note: Some consider measuring biodiversity in credit and debit units impossible or reject it on ethical grounds.

title: No net loss

definition.text: An environmental policy approach that aims to balance out a development's harm to the environment through mitigation measures.

facts.text: It began in the US in the 1980s as a goal for wetland conservation; George H. W. Bush promised "no net loss of wetlands" in his 1988 campaign.
It is now an objective for biodiversity offsetting in many countries, and by 2018 was in place in at least 69.
It is applied through Environmental Impact Assessments using the mitigation hierarchy.
Lenders such as the International Finance Corporation require it on projects they co-finance.
A study of US mitigation banking found it was producing a net loss of wetland area nationally.
A study of a Victorian (Australia) scheme found up to 86% of offsets did not make up for losses of native vegetation.
There is no agreed metric for measuring losses and gains, and baselines are often undefined.

contested_note: Some reject no net loss as impossible or unacceptable for ecological, social or cultural reasons, while others see it as a way to reconcile development with conservation.

definition.text: A goal under which a project's environmental gains from mitigation outweigh its harms, leaving more biodiversity than before.

facts.text: Net gain or net positive impact is used instead of no net loss when the aim is to leave biodiversity better than before.
England's Biodiversity Net Gain policy requires a 10% net gain compared with the previous state.
Net positive impact usually applies to a single development project, while no net loss is applied at many geographic scales.
No net loss aims to cancel out biodiversity loss, while net positive impact aims for a net gain.

definition.text: Rules that set how much habitat must be credited for each unit of damage (mitigation ratios) and require offsets to match or exceed the biodiversity lost (like-for-like).

facts.text: Credit ratios have been proposed as a way to deal with uncertainty in offsetting.
A coverage ratio of 3:1 requires 3 compensatory mitigation credits for each unit of ecological damage.
Uganda's law requires offsets to follow the "like-for-like or better" principle; China's eco-compensation does not require like-for-like offsets.
Friends of the Earth argues that like-for-like compensation of lost biodiversity may not be possible.

title: Safe harbor agreement
article: Endangered Species Act of 1973#Safe Harbor Agreements

definition.text: A voluntary US agreement in which a landowner improves land for a listed species and in return is allowed some future harm to that species.

facts.text: It covers species already listed as threatened or endangered under the Endangered Species Act.
The policy was developed under the Clinton administration; the Environmental Defense Fund designed the plan in 1995 to give landowners incentives to help endangered species.
In 2024 it was merged with another programme into Conservation Benefits Agreements.
Unlike a habitat conservation plan, the activities a Safe Harbor Agreement covers are designed to protect species.

distinct_from: Perverse incentives of endangered species protection
notes: US-specific tool under the Endangered Species Act; kept as a Minor example of incentive-based species conservation.
